title: Capstone I: Task manager core
subtitle: Design and build the heart of a real app
goal: Design and build the core of a task manager: dataclass models, a validating service layer, JSON storage and a unit test suite.
outcomes: Turn requirements into models, services and storage
Model data with dataclasses, enums and to_dict/from_dict
Enforce rules in a service layer with domain exceptions
Store data in JSON atomically and handle corrupt files
Prove behaviour with a unittest suite

slides.title: Mission 58: Capstone, part one
slides.body:
Two days, one real application: **Kaam**, a command-line task manager you can show in interviews.

Today: the core (models, rules, storage and tests). Tomorrow: the command line, polish and shipping.
slides.say: Welcome to the capstone. Over two days you build Kaam, a real task manager that you can put on GitHub and talk about in interviews. Today you build its core, the way professionals do: requirements first, then the data model, the service layer with its rules, storage on disk, and tests that prove it all works. Tomorrow you ship it.

slides.title: Requirements first
slides.body: Before code, write down what users need, then what each need becomes in code. This table is your plan for two days.

head: Users need to…
In code
rows: Add a task: title, due date, priority
Never save junk (empty titles, bad dates)
See open tasks, most urgent first

slides.say: Professionals start with requirements, not code. A user must be able to add a task with a title, an optional due date and a priority, see open tasks with the most urgent first, mark tasks done, delete them, and find everything still there tomorrow. Next to each need, we write the piece of code that will deliver it. That table is our plan.

slides.title: The architecture
slides.body: Same layers as Day 55, one module per job. `errors.py` holds **KaamError** and its children: `ValidationError`, `TaskNotFound`, `StorageError`.
slides.say: Kaam uses the layers from day fifty five. Models dot p y holds the data classes. Errors dot p y holds one base exception, Kaam error, with specific children for validation, missing tasks and storage problems. Storage dot p y saves and loads. Services dot p y holds the rules. Tomorrow, c l i dot p y becomes the interface. Each file has exactly one job.

slides.title: The model: an enum and a dataclass
slides.body: An `Enum` makes invalid priorities impossible. `to_dict()` converts to JSON-friendly values for storage.
slides.code:
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from datetime import date
from enum import Enum

class Priority(Enum):
    LOW = 1
    MEDIUM = 2
    HIGH = 3

@dataclass
class Task:
    id: int
    title: str
    priority: Priority = Priority.MEDIUM
    due: date | None = None
    done: bool = False
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        data = asdict(self)
        data["priority"] = self.priority.name.lower()
        data["due"] = self.due.isoformat() if self.due else None
        return data

task = Task(1, "Pay electricity bill", Priority.HIGH, date(2026, 10, 25), tags=["home"])
print(task)
print(task.to_dict())
slides.expect:
Task(id=1, title='Pay electricity bill', priority=<Priority.HIGH: 3>, due=datetime.date(2026, 10, 25), done=False, tags=['home'])
{'id': 1, 'title': 'Pay electricity bill', 'priority': 'high', 'due': '2026-10-25', 'done': False, 'tags': ['home']}
explain: Enum members have a name and a value; HIGH > LOW by value.
date | None: a due date is optional.
default_factory=list: every task gets its own new list.
asdict converts the dataclass into a dict.
Store the enum as plain text: 'high'.
slides.say: Priority is an enum, so a typo like hihg is impossible. Task is a dataclass with sensible defaults: medium priority, no due date, not done, and an empty tag list made fresh for every task. To dict turns a task into plain JSON friendly values, so the enum becomes the word high and the date becomes text.

slides.title: Predict: why default_factory?
slides.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Task:
    title: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

a, b = Task("Buy milk"), Task("Call bank")
a.tags.append("home")
print(a.tags, b.tags)
slides.why: `default_factory=list` calls `list()` for **each** new Task, so every task has its own list. (A plain `tags: list = []` is refused by dataclasses for exactly this reason: the mutable default trap from Day 18.)
slides.say: Remember the mutable default trap from day eighteen? Two tasks, and we add a tag to only the first one. What do both tag lists look like?

slides.solution:
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from datetime import date
from enum import Enum


class Priority(Enum):
    LOW = 1
    MEDIUM = 2
    HIGH = 3


@dataclass
class Task:
    id: int
    title: str
    priority: Priority = Priority.MEDIUM
    due: date | None = None
    done: bool = False
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        data = asdict(self)
        data["priority"] = self.priority.name.lower()
        data["due"] = self.due.isoformat() if self.due else None
        return data

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data: dict) -> "Task":
        due = data.get("due")
        return cls(
            id=data["id"],
            title=data["title"],
            priority=Priority[data.get("priority", "medium").upper()],
            due=date.fromisoformat(due) if due else None,
            done=data.get("done", False),
            tags=list(data.get("tags", [])),
        )


print(Task.from_dict({"id": 7, "title": "Call bank", "priority": "high", "due": "2026-10-25"}))
slides.tests:
from datetime import date
original = Task(3, "Renew passport", Priority.HIGH, date(2026, 11, 30), done=True, tags=["govt", "travel"])
back = Task.from_dict(original.to_dict())
assert back == original, "Task.from_dict(task.to_dict()) should give back an equal Task. Got " + repr(back)
assert isinstance(back.due, date) and back.priority is Priority.HIGH, "due must become a date and priority a Priority member, not strings."
minimal = Task.from_dict({"id": 9, "title": "Buy milk"})
assert minimal == Task(9, "Buy milk"), "Missing fields should get the defaults (MEDIUM, None, False, []). Got " + repr(minimal)
assert Task.from_dict({"id": 1, "title": "x", "priority": "High"}).priority is Priority.HIGH, "Accept any case: 'High' should become Priority.HIGH."
assert Task.from_dict({"id": 1, "title": "x", "due": None}).due is None, "A due of None should stay None."
slides.say: Your first capstone task. Storage will save tasks as dictionaries, so we need the reverse of to dict. Finish from dict: turn the priority text back into the enum, whatever its case, turn the date text back into a real date, and give any missing fields their defaults. The tests check a full round trip and a minimal record.

slides.title: The service layer: rules live here
slides.body: `TaskService` receives a storage object and enforces every rule. It **never prints** and **never touches files** directly; it raises `KaamError`s instead.

nodes.t: Title, priority and date all valid?
nodes.yes: build Task with the next id

slides.say: The service layer is the heart of Kaam. Task service receives a storage object from outside, and every rule lives here: titles must be one to eighty characters, priorities must exist, dates must be real dates, and IDs are assigned automatically. It never prints and never opens files. When something is wrong, it raises one of our Kaam errors.

slides.title: TaskService.add
slides.body: `models.py` (with your `from_dict`), `errors.py` and `storage.py` sit next to this file. `MemoryStorage` keeps tasks as dicts in memory: ideal for trying things and for tests.
slides.code:
from errors import ValidationError
from models import Priority, Task
from storage import MemoryStorage

class TaskService:
    def __init__(self, storage):
        self.storage = storage

    def add(self, title: str, priority: str = "medium") -> Task:
        title = title.strip()
        if not 1 <= len(title) <= 80:
            raise ValidationError("title must be 1 to 80 characters")
        tasks = self.storage.load()
        next_id = max((t.id for t in tasks), default=0) + 1
        task = Task(next_id, title, Priority[priority.upper()])
        self.storage.save(tasks + [task])
        return task

service = TaskService(MemoryStorage())
print(service.add("Pay electricity bill", "high"))
print(service.add("  Renew passport  "))
try:
    service.add("   ")
except ValidationError as err:
    print("rejected:", err)
slides.expect:
Task(id=1, title='Pay electricity bill', priority=<Priority.HIGH: 3>, due=None, done=False, tags=[])
Task(id=2, title='Renew passport', priority=<Priority.MEDIUM: 2>, due=None, done=False, tags=[])
rejected: title must be 1 to 80 characters
explain: The storage is injected: memory today, JSON in production.
Rules raise domain exceptions; the service never prints.
max(..., default=0) handles the very first task.

Then it loads the current tasks, picks the next ID, builds the task and saves the new list. The demo uses memory storage, so nothing touches the disk. Notice how the blank title is rejected with a clear message.

slides.title: Quick check: why inject storage?
slides.q: Why does `TaskService` take `storage` as a parameter instead of creating a `JsonStorage` itself?
options: So tests can pass `MemoryStorage` and production can pass `JsonStorage`, with no change to the service
Because Python requires every class to take a parameter
It makes the service run faster
slides.why: Dependency injection (Day 54): the service depends on "something with load and save", not on a specific file. Tests stay fast and never touch your real tasks.
slides.say: Task service could create its own JSON storage. Instead, it receives storage from outside. Why is that the better design?

slides.title: Your turn: validate priority and due date
slides.task:
`add` crashes on bad input. Make it raise **`ValidationError`** instead:
- an unknown priority (like `"urgent"`) must not leak a `KeyError`
- `due` is `None` or text like `"2026-10-25"`: convert it with `date.fromisoformat`; bad text (`"25/10/2026"`, `"2026-02-30"`) is a `ValidationError`
- nothing is saved when validation fails

from datetime import date

from errors import ValidationError
from models import Priority, Task
from storage import MemoryStorage

class TaskService:
    def __init__(self, storage):
        self.storage = storage

    def add(self, title: str, priority: str = "medium", due: str | None = None) -> Task:
        title = title.strip()
        if not 1 <= len(title) <= 80:
            raise ValidationError("title must be 1 to 80 characters")
        level = Priority[priority.upper()]     # TODO: unknown priority -> ValidationError
        due_date = due                         # TODO: text -> date; None stays None; bad -> ValidationError
        tasks = self.storage.load()
        task = Task(max((t.id for t in tasks), default=0) + 1, title, level, due_date)
        self.storage.save(tasks + [task])
        return task

service = TaskService(MemoryStorage())
print(service.add("Call plumber", "low"))

from datetime import date
from errors import ValidationError
from models import Priority
from storage import MemoryStorage
store = MemoryStorage()
service = TaskService(store)
try:
    t = service.add("Pay electricity bill", "HIGH", "2026-10-25")
except Exception as err:
    raise AssertionError("add('Pay electricity bill', 'HIGH', '2026-10-25') crashed with " + type(err).__name__ + ": " + str(err) + ". Convert the due text with date.fromisoformat().")
assert t.priority is Priority.HIGH and t.due == date(2026, 10, 25), "Expected priority HIGH and due date(2026, 10, 25). Got " + repr(t)
t2 = service.add("Call plumber")
assert t2.due is None and t2.priority is Priority.MEDIUM, "With no due date, due should stay None and priority default to MEDIUM."
cases = [({"priority": "urgent"}, "an unknown priority"), ({"due": "25/10/2026"}, "a date that isn't YYYY-MM-DD"), ({"due": "2026-02-30"}, "an impossible date (30 February)")]
for kwargs, what in cases:
    try:
        service.add("Bad task", **kwargs)
    except ValidationError:
        pass
    except Exception as err:
        raise AssertionError("add with " + what + " raised " + type(err).__name__ + ". Catch it and raise ValidationError instead, so the CLI can show a friendly message.")
    else:
        raise AssertionError("add with " + what + " should raise ValidationError.")
assert [t.id for t in store.load()] == [1, 2], "Rejected tasks must not be saved. Validate everything before saving."

`date.fromisoformat("2026-02-30")` raises `ValueError`: catch it the same way.

slides.title: Storage: same interface, two backends
slides.body:
`JsonStorage` offers the **same two methods** as `MemoryStorage`: `load()` and `save(tasks)`. The service cannot tell them apart (duck typing).

Save **atomically**: write a temporary file, then `os.replace` it, so a crash mid-write never leaves a half-written file.

left.title: MemoryStorage

right.title: JsonStorage

visual.verdict: Same methods, different backend: swap one for the other without touching the service.

slides.say: Json storage offers exactly the same two methods as memory storage, load and save, so the service cannot tell them apart. That is duck typing. One important detail: save atomically. Write to a temporary file first, then swap it into place with os dot replace. If the power cuts out halfway through a write, your old file is still intact.

slides.title: JsonStorage with atomic writes
slides.code:
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

from models import Priority, Task

class JsonStorage:
    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = Path(path)

    def load(self) -> list[Task]:
        if not self.path.exists():
            return []
        rows = json.loads(self.path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        return [Task.from_dict(row) for row in rows]

    def save(self, tasks: list[Task]) -> None:
        tmp = self.path.with_suffix(".tmp")
        tmp.write_text(json.dumps([t.to_dict() for t in tasks], indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
        os.replace(tmp, self.path)          # atomic: never a half-written file

store = JsonStorage("tasks.json")
store.save([Task(1, "Pay electricity bill", Priority.HIGH), Task(2, "Call plumber", tags=["home"])])
print(Path("tasks.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print(store.load()[1])

slides.title: Predict: JSON and dates
slides.code:
import json
from datetime import date

print(json.dumps({"title": "Pay bill", "due": date(2026, 10, 25)}))
options: TypeError: Object of type date is not JSON serializable
slides.why: JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, lists and objects. A `date` (or an `Enum`) must be converted first, which is exactly why `Task.to_dict()` exists.
slides.say: JSON knows text, numbers, true and false, null, lists and objects. What happens when you hand it a Python date?

slides.title: Your turn: storage that fails well
slides.task:
Make `JsonStorage.load()` robust:
- a **missing** file means no tasks yet: return `[]`
- **broken** JSON, or a row that can't become a Task, raises `StorageError` whose message names the file
- `save` then `load` still round-trips

`tasks.json` and `old.json` next to this program are both broken.

slides.title: Project: finish the Kaam core
slides.brief: `add` is done. Finish the rest of `TaskService` so Kaam can run a real to-do list. `models.py`, `errors.py` and `storage.py` sit next to your file.
steps: `complete(task_id)`: load, find the task, set `done = True`, save, return it
`delete(task_id)`: load, find it, save the list **without** it, return it
Unknown ids raise `TaskNotFound` (write one `_find` helper and use it twice)
`pending()`: open tasks only, sorted by priority (high first), then due date (no date last), then id
`due_soon(today, days=3)`: pending tasks due on or before `today + days`, overdue ones included

from datetime import date
from errors import TaskNotFound
from storage import MemoryStorage
store = MemoryStorage()
s = TaskService(store)
s.add("Pay electricity bill", "high", "2026-10-25")   # 1
s.add("Renew passport", "medium", "2026-11-30")       # 2
s.add("Call plumber", "low")                          # 3
s.add("Book Tatkal ticket", "high", "2026-10-21")     # 4
s.add("Buy diyas", "medium", "2026-10-19")            # 5
order = [t.id for t in s.pending()]
assert order == [4, 1, 5, 2, 3], "pending() should order by priority (high first), then due date, then id: expected ids [4, 1, 5, 2, 3], got " + str(order)
done = s.complete(4)
assert done is not None and done.id == 4 and done.done, "complete(4) should return task 4 with done=True."
assert any(t.id == 4 and t.done for t in store.load()), "complete() must save the change through self.storage.save(...)."
assert [t.id for t in s.pending()] == [1, 5, 2, 3], "Completed tasks should disappear from pending()."
soon = [t.id for t in s.due_soon(date(2026, 10, 22), days=3)]
assert soon == [1, 5], "On 22 Oct with days=3: task 1 (due 25 Oct) and overdue task 5 (19 Oct), in pending order. Got " + str(soon)
removed = s.delete(3)
assert removed is not None and removed.title == "Call plumber", "delete(3) should return the deleted task."
assert 3 not in [t.id for t in store.load()], "delete() must save the list without the task."
for action in (s.complete, s.delete):
    try:
        action(99)
    except TaskNotFound:
        pass
    else:
        raise AssertionError(action.__name__ + "(99) should raise TaskNotFound: there is no task 99.")

        data["due"] = self.due.isoformat() if self.due else None
        return data

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data: dict) -> "Task":
        due = data.get("due")
        return cls(
            id=data["id"],
            title=data["title"],
            priority=Priority[data.get("priority", "medium").upper()],
            due=date.fromisoformat(due) if due else None,
            done=data.get("done", False),
            tags=list(data.get("tags", [])),
        )

slides.code:
import io
import unittest

from errors import TaskNotFound, ValidationError
from services import TaskService
from storage import MemoryStorage

class TaskServiceTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.service = TaskService(MemoryStorage())

    def test_add_assigns_increasing_ids(self):
        ids = [self.service.add(title).id for title in ("A", "B", "C")]
        self.assertEqual(ids, [1, 2, 3])

    def test_blank_title_is_rejected(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValidationError):
            self.service.add("   ")

    def test_complete_unknown_task(self):
        with self.assertRaises(TaskNotFound):
            self.service.complete(42)

    def test_pending_most_urgent_first(self):
        self.service.add("Low one", "low")
        self.service.add("Urgent", "high", due="2026-10-20")
        self.assertEqual([t.title for t in self.service.pending()], ["Urgent", "Low one"])

suite = unittest.defaultTestLoader.loadTestsFromTestCase(TaskServiceTests)
result = unittest.TextTestRunner(stream=io.StringIO()).run(suite)
print(f"ran {result.testsRun} tests: {len(result.failures)} failures, {len(result.errors)} errors")
print("OK" if result.wasSuccessful() else "FAILED")
explain: setUp runs before every test: a fresh, empty service each time.
One behaviour per test, named like a sentence.

Run quietly and print our own summary.

from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass, field
from datetime import date
from enum import Enum


class Priority(Enum):
    LOW = 1
    MEDIUM = 2
    HIGH = 3


@dataclass
class Task:
    id: int
    title: str
    priority: Priority = Priority.MEDIUM
    due: date | None = None
    done: bool = False
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

    def to_dict(self) -> dict:
        data = asdict(self)
        data["priority"] = self.priority.name.lower()
        data["due"] = self.due.isoformat() if self.due else None
        return data

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data: dict) -> "Task":
        due = data.get("due")
        return cls(
            id=data["id"],
            title=data["title"],
            priority=Priority[data.get("priority", "medium").upper()],
            due=date.fromisoformat(due) if due else None,
            done=data.get("done", False),
            tags=list(data.get("tags", [])),
        )
